Let me analyze these teaching examples carefully to identify systematic errors in the forecasts compared to true outcomes.

Looking at the data patterns:

## Example 1 (2025-11-05)
- History is around 78-82 range, showing some volatility
- Model forecasts are generally higher than true outcomes by about 0.1-0.3 on average
- Looking at the first few points: 
  - Model: [81.68, 80.56, 79.91, 80.32, 80.86, 81.82, 81.04, 80.58, 79.57, 80.72]
  - True: [81.49, 80.17, 79.47, 79.96, 80.65, 81.91, 81.34, 80.93, 79.92, 81.22]
  
The model is consistently under-forecasting by about 0.15-0.25 on average in the early horizon, but this narrows as we go further out.

## Example 2 (2025-11-04)
Very similar to Example 1, with slightly more divergence initially but converging at longer horizons.

## Example 3 (2025-10-27)
Slightly different history (last price is 78.32 instead of 78.44 on 11-05)
Model forecasts are again slightly above true outcomes by ~0.05-0.15

## Example 4 (2025-10-24)
Model forecasts are again close but slightly high by ~0.05-0.10

## Example 5 (2025-10-28)
Model forecasts are again slightly high by ~0.05-0.10

## Sentiment Analysis
Looking at sentiment history:
- When sentiment is high (1.00), prices tend to be lower than expected or are mean-reverting


- Low sentiment (0.00 or 0.33) correlates with prices being near the lower end of the range
- The model struggles to accurately predict prices when sentiment shifts between low and high

I notice a consistent pattern of mild forecast bias, particularly around sentiment changes. The model tends to be slightly too optimistic, especially when sentiment transitions between low and high ranges. Mean reversion appears to play a role, with prices naturally gravitating toward the middle of their historical range.

The key observations point to nuanced corrections needed when sentiment fluctuates
